query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a single tailored thermo‐mechanical processing step—specifically, cryogenic rolling followed by controlled annealing—to a cast eutectic high‐entropy alloy (EHEA) with a dual-phase lamellar structure will refine its microstructure to an ultrafine duplex state that simultaneously boosts both strength and ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with a dual-phase, lamellar microstructure (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1 or a similar EHEA) containing soft FCC and hard BCC/intermetallic phases.
generation.intervention: Cryogenic rolling (cryo-rolling) followed by an optimized annealing treatment.
generation.conditions: Processing performed at cryogenic temperatures followed by annealing under controlled conditions; mechanical testing (e.g., tensile tests) conducted at room temperature, where the effects of the refined microstructure are expected to manifest.
generation.structural_mediator: An ultrafine duplex microstructure with refined lamellar interfaces, enhanced grain boundary density, and activated nano-twinning which together provide distributed load sharing and improved dislocation storage.
generation.mechanism: The intervention refines the lamellar structure, increases the density of phase interfaces, and promotes the formation of beneficial deformation mechanisms (such as nano-twinning) that serve both to strengthen the material (via grain boundary and interface strengthening) and to enhance ductility by arresting microcrack propagation and enabling steady plastic flow.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast state, the treated EHEA will exhibit a simultaneous increase in yield/ultimate tensile strength (potentially by a notable margin, as indicated by previous studies reporting improvements up to ~50% in similar alloys) and enhanced ductility (improved elongation by maintaining a better strain hardening response).
generation.baseline: The as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with its original dual-phase lamellar microstructure, which typically shows a trade-off between strength and ductility.
generation.boundary: This effect is anticipated to hold for eutectic HEAs with dual-phase lamellar microstructures; the magnitude of the improvements may be sensitive to processing parameters, alloy composition, and scale of the microstructural features.
generation.uncertainty: While previous evidence (e.g., improvements reported after cryo-rolling and annealing in EHEAs) supports the viability of the approach, the exact quantitative improvement in strength and ductility and the interplay of deformation mechanisms (e.g., nano-twinning vs. dislocation accumulation) remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same as-cast eutectic HEA. Subject one set to the cryogenic rolling followed by controlled annealing treatment, while keeping the other set as a control (no additional processing). Conduct standardized room-temperature tensile tests on both sets. Characterize the resulting microstructure (e.g., using electron microscopy) and quantify mechanical properties.
measurements: Microstructural characterization (lamellar thickness, grain size, twin density)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cryo-rolled and annealed samples do not show a statistically significant simultaneous increase in both strength (e.g., yield and ultimate tensile strength) and ductility (elongation) relative to the as-cast control samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism. This work provides a pathway for strengthening eutectic alloys and widens the design toolbox for high-performance materials based upon EHEAs. To tackle the aforementioned problems, eutectic HEAs (EHEAs) [] were proposed. On the one hand, EHEAs should have the general character of traditional eutectic alloys. In this sense, EHEAs should have better fluidity and thus better castability and less casting defects [,]. On the other hand, EHEAs as one kind of in-situ composites with lamellar or rod-like eutectic microstructures might reach the balance between strength and ductility via mixing the soft FCC phase with the hard BCC phase or intermetallic compound [,,,,,,,,]. Some EHEAs indeed have outstanding properties. Lu et al. [] reported the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA with simultaneous high strength (944 MPa) and good ductility (25.6%). The excellent mechanical properties do not depend significantly on derivation of eutectic compositions []. After cold-rolling and annealing, its strength reached up to 1.2 GPa and its elongation could remain at about 12% []. After cryo-rolling and annealing, its strength could reach up to 1.47 GPa while its ductility could even increase to 14% []. He et al. [,] designed the CoCrFeNiNbx EHEAs and found that the microstructures were stable from 600 °C to 900 °C.
